title: Data Engineering & Big Data
summary: The plumbing that moves raw events into clean, queryable data — and the few ideas (MapReduce, Spark, lakehouses) that make it work across thousands of machines.

blocks.markdown:
Data engineering builds the pipelines that move raw data to where people can query it.

- Four stages, always: **ingest → store → process → serve**.
- **"Big data"** just means it's too big or too fast for one machine, so you spread the work.
- The core trick: split data into piles, process each independently, then stitch results back by key.
- Hadoop, Spark, warehouses, and streaming are all variations on *how to split, store, and move the piles*.

blocks.subTitle: What to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Pick the tool by latency, cost, and how raw the data is.

| When you want | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Results every few hours | Batch (Spark) |
| Reaction in seconds | Streaming (Kafka + Flink) |
| Cheap raw storage | Data lake (S3 + Parquet) |
| Fast governed SQL | Warehouse (Snowflake) |
| SQL **and** ML, cheaply | Lakehouse (Iceberg/Delta) |

blocks.subTitle: Why distributed at all
blocks.markdown:
Three hard constraints forced every idea in this topic.

- **Storage doesn't fit one box.** A petabyte needs thousands of disks, so data is spread and replicated.
- **Move compute to the data.** The network is ~100x slower than local disk, so ship the *code* to where data sits.
- **Failure is normal.** With 10,000 disks, several die daily — the framework must silently re-run lost work.

Google's 2004 MapReduce paper packaged all three so you only write two simple functions.

blocks.subTitle: The MapReduce mental model
blocks.markdown:
Word count is the canonical example: count every word in a terabyte of text.

![MapReduce word count: map, shuffle, reduce](assets/data-engineering-big-data/mapreduce-wordcount.svg)

- **Map** — each chunk emits `(word, 1)` pairs, with no coordination. Embarrassingly parallel.
- **Shuffle** — the framework groups pairs by key so every `(cat, 1)` lands on the same reducer.
- **Reduce** — each reducer sums its key's list: `(cat, [1,1,1]) → (cat, 3)`.
- The **shuffle moves data over the network** and is where most jobs spend their time.

assets.alt: MapReduce word count: map, shuffle, reduce

blocks.subTitle: Why Spark beat Hadoop
blocks.markdown:
Classic MapReduce wrote every step to disk; a 5-step job meant 5 slow round-trips.

- **In-memory.** Spark keeps intermediates in RAM between steps — ~100x faster for iterative work.
- **Lazy DAG.** It plans the whole job as a graph and optimizes across steps before running anything.
- **RDD lineage.** Each dataset records the recipe that built it, so a lost partition is recomputed, not the whole job.
- One engine for batch, SQL, streaming, and ML — commonly **10–100x** faster than MapReduce.

blocks.subTitle: OLTP vs OLAP & columnar
blocks.markdown:
Different query shapes want different storage layouts.

- **OLTP** (Postgres, MySQL) — many tiny reads/writes for apps; stores data **row-by-row** so whole records sit together.
- **OLAP** (analytics) — few huge scans over many rows but few columns; stores data **column-by-column**.
- Columnar lets a query read **only the columns it needs** and skip the rest.
- Columns also **compress far better** — adjacent values (all dates, one country) squash down tightly.

blocks.subTitle: Partitioning & Parquet
blocks.markdown:
Two cheap wins beat every other analytics optimization.

- **Partitioning** splits data into folders by a column, usually date (`/year=2025/month=06/`). A June query opens only the June folder — **partition pruning**.
- **Parquet** is the standard columnar format: per-column compression plus per-chunk **min/max stats**.
- Those stats let the reader skip whole chunks that can't match a filter — **predicate pushdown**.
- Together they routinely cut bytes scanned — and cost — by **10x or more**.

blocks.subTitle: Batch vs streaming
blocks.markdown:
The two processing styles differ in how the data arrives.

![Batch pipeline versus streaming pipeline](assets/data-engineering-big-data/batch-vs-streaming.svg)

- **Batch** runs a bounded chunk ("yesterday's events") to completion on a schedule. High throughput, trivial to re-run, latency in minutes-to-hours.
- **Streaming** processes an unbounded flow as events arrive — latency in seconds, but genuinely harder.
- It must hold **state** across events (windows) and handle out-of-order arrivals.
- **Event time vs processing time**: when it happened vs when you saw it. A **watermark** estimates "all events up to T have arrived" to finalize a window.

blocks.subTitle: Warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse
blocks.markdown:
All three store analytics data — they trade governance against cost.

![Warehouse versus lake versus lakehouse](assets/data-engineering-big-data/warehouse-lake-lakehouse.svg)

- **Warehouse** — structured, **schema-on-write**, fast governed SQL, pricey.
- **Lake** — raw files on cheap object storage, **schema-on-read**, flexible but easily a "data swamp."
- **Lakehouse** — a table format (Iceberg, Delta) on lake storage adds **ACID, schema enforcement, time travel**.
- The lakehouse is literally an attempt to get warehouse guarantees at the lake's price.

blocks.subTitle: ETL vs ELT and rules of thumb
blocks.markdown:
Where you transform decides ETL vs ELT.

- **ETL** transforms *before* loading — the old default when warehouse storage was scarce.
- **ELT** loads raw first, transforms *inside* the warehouse (often via dbt) — the modern default, since storage and compute are cheap.

Deciding:
- A few minutes of delay OK? **Prefer batch** — cheaper and simpler.
- Unsure what you'll need later? **Land it raw in a lake** — you can't recover discarded data.
- Don't reach for Spark until one machine genuinely can't cope.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
A handful of systems show up in nearly every pipeline.

- **Kafka** — a distributed append-only log; the ingest backbone. One event stream feeds fraud, batch, and analytics independently ([messaging-streaming](messaging-streaming)).
- **Spark** — the default processing engine: in-memory, DAG optimizer, lineage recovery.
- **BigQuery / Snowflake** — warehouses that **separate storage from compute**, so you scale and pay for each independently.
- **Iceberg / Delta** — table formats over Parquet on S3 that add ACID and time travel.

blocks.subTitle: A daily revenue pipeline
blocks.markdown:
Daily revenue per country from a raw order stream, expressed in Spark.

```python
orders  = read_parquet("s3://lake/orders/raw/year=2025/month=06/day=18/")
clean   = orders.filter(lambda o: o.status == "completed" and o.amount > 0)
by_cty  = clean.map(lambda o: (o.country, o.amount))   # key by country
revenue = by_cty.reduceByKey(lambda a, b: a + b)        # shuffle + sum
revenue.write_parquet("s3://lake/orders/agg/day=2025-06-18/")
```

- It reads **only yesterday's partition** — partition pruning skips 364 other days.
- Filtering early means the shuffle moves kilobytes, not the full terabyte.
- This is plain MapReduce: `map` keys by country, `reduceByKey` shuffles and sums.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production.

- **"Big data means Spark."** It means data won't fit one machine. Tens of GB? Postgres or DuckDB is simpler.
- **"Streaming is just faster batch."** It's a harder model — stateful windows, late events, always-on infra.
- **"A lake is automatically better."** Without governance it rots into a swamp nobody trusts.
- **"ELT is always better than ETL."** Transform first when scrubbing PII or shrinking volume.
- **"Partition later."** It's the *first*, cheapest big win — retrofitting means rewriting the dataset.
